newsitem.title: USA: Stock market up but banking stocks down after Fed move.
newsitem.headline: Stock market up but banking stocks down after Fed move.

text.p: The stock market improved Wednesday, helped by a quick recovery by battered technology stocks, but bank stocks fell a day after the Federal Reserve raised interest rates for the first time in more than two years.

The dollar was mixed against major currencies despite early gains on surprisingly robust U.S. manufacturing data. In commodity markets, coffee futures rose on supply concerns and gold rose on questions about the size of an Indonesian find.
The Dow Jones industrial average closed up 4.53 points at 6,880.70, while the technology-laden Nasdaq Composite index jumped 21.02 points to 1,269.08.
In the broader market, advancing issues led declines 1,302 to 1,148 on active volume of 487 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
"For the first time in quite a while, the big tech stocks pulled up the Nasdaq," said Alfred Kugel, senior investment strategist at Stein Roe & Farnham.
For the most part, though, the rebound in companies like Microsoft Corp., Intel Corp. and International Business Machines Corp. did not spread to the rest of the market.
"We had a reversal in the malaise in the technology sector, but it did not rub off on the rest of the market," said Kugel.

Kugel said the market would remain in its current range, saying it was in a "digestion period" after a surge in corporate earnings and a stronger-than-expected economy that stretched from last November to mid-February.
Wall Street also pondered Tuesday's rise in interest rates by the Fed, and the latest economic data fanned expectations of further monetary tightening to slow the economy's growth.
The Commerce Department said durable goods orders rose 1.5 percent in February, contrasting with analysts' expectations for a 0.4 percent drop after January's strong gain of 4.1 percent.
The unexpected February orders pickup suggests the economy's industrial sector remains vigorous and may be gaining momentum.

On Tuesday, the Fed raised short-term interest rates by a quarter percentage point. It described the move -- the first since February 1995 -- as a "prudent step" designed to help prolong the economic expansion by keeping inflation low through the end of next year.

The interest-rate hike will mean higher borrowing costs for consumer and corporate loans. Many commercial banks, including Chase Manhattan, the nation's largest bank, boosted their lending rates in response to the Fed move.
Investors are worried the action could hurt corporate profits as consumers cut back on spending.

In the bond market, the key 30-year Treasury bond was off 6/32, or $1.875 on a $1,000 bond, raising its yield to 6.98 percent from 6.97 percent at Tuesday's close. Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions.
In currency markets, the dollar hit session highs against the German mark and Japanese yen shortly after the Commerce Department report.

But the dollar succumbed to profit-taking in light afternoon trading to close slightly lower at 1.6887 marks from Tuesday's close of 1.6903 and well below its 1.6955 session high. Against the yen, the dollar closed below its 124.47 session high at 124.18, but held above Tuesday's 123.70 close.
At New York's Coffee Sugar and Cocoa Exchange, coffee futures rose on concerns about supplies and tight roaster stockpiles. Coffee for May delivery closed up 7.55 cents a pound at 186.85 cents.
"Stocks have only moved up marginally, and producers are virtually sold out," said Merrill Lynch analyst Judith Ganes.

At the Commodity Exchange in New York, gold prices closed higher on news that a huge gold find in Indonesia may have been overstated and on sentiment that gold fell too sharply on Tuesday's interest rate hike by the Federal Reserve.
June gold closed $3 an ounce higher at $353.50 an ounce.
In overseas trading, London's benchmark FTSE 100 index added 30.8 points to 4,301.5. In Tokyo, the 225-share Nikkei average ended 32.84 points or 0.18 percent higher at 18,472.45.
